pathway.title: American Airlines, Inc. — Credit Snapshot
pathway.question: Should we own this issuer, in which instrument, and why?

runs.text: First, earnings are the pressure point, not liquidity. Revenue grew 19.3% in the third quarter of 2026 to USD 16,335 million, but fuel expense rose USD 1,868 million to USD 4,635 million and operating income fell to USD 115 million from USD 151 million; the pre-tax loss widened to USD 334 million from USD 142 million (Documentary Fact; CP-1 table). Nine-month operating income was USD 521 million against USD 1,015 million a year earlier. The mechanism is that the company carries no fuel hedges and recaptures higher fuel only through fares, so a fuel move reaches operating income and cash flow within the same quarter (Documentary Fact; CP-1A operating model).

Second, leverage is high on every measure the sources allow. Management's own net debt was USD 28,079 million at September 30, 2026, up from USD 27,438 million at March 31, 2026; against last-twelve-month EBITDAR built from income statement lines of USD 4,127 million that is 6.80x, versus management's stated target of 3.0x (Documentary Fact for the debt figures, Analyst Interpretation for the ratio; CP-1 calculation C13). The ratio omits regional depreciation and rent, so management's own adjusted measure would differ, but the gap to the target is large on any definition the sources support. This also corrects a garbled bullet in the CP-1 handoff, which should have said that net debt rose between those dates.

Third, debt service rests on liquidity and refinancing access more than on earnings. Last-twelve-month operating income of USD 973 million was below net interest expense of USD 1,664 million, and last-twelve-month free cash flow on a simple definition was negative USD 91 million (Documentary Fact; CP-1 calculations C6 and C8). Nine-month operating cash flow of USD 4,541 million was helped by a rise in air traffic and loyalty liabilities, and the derived third-quarter operating cash flow was negative USD 153 million with third-quarter capex of USD 1,095 million (Analyst Interpretation; CP-1 calculation C7). Customer-funded float lifts liquidity in good quarters and unwinds when bookings or mileage sales slow.

Fourth, the maturity profile is manageable near term and concentrated in 2028. American's principal due is USD 631 million for the remainder of 2026, USD 3,550 million in 2027 and USD 7,861 million in 2028, the peak year, against USD 11,797 million of AAG liquidity (Documentary Fact; CP-1 table). Nearly 87% of Note 5 debt is secured (CP-1 calculation C11), and 2026 refinancings pushed the 2014 term loans to May 2033 and revolvers to March 2031, so refinancing depends mainly on asset-backed markets for aircraft and loyalty collateral (Documentary Fact; CP-1A transaction summary). Nothing in the supplied sources shows how much headroom those collateral pools have.

Fifth, the business has real franchise support. Cash from co-branded credit card and other partners was USD 6,200 million in 2025, Citi became exclusive issuer of the co-branded portfolio in 2026, and premium and corporate revenue are growing per management (Documentary Fact for the partner cash, Management Language for the premium claims; CP-1A operating model). That cash is also the collateral base of the AAdvantage Financing, so it supports both revenue durability and secured borrowing capacity.

Sixth, structure matters for this issuer. The three PSP promissory notes of USD 3,746 million are the only unsecured debt and sit at the AAG parent, while American itself carries USD 25,876 million of debt and finance leases and a USD 10,430 million receivable from related parties (Documentary Fact; CP-1 table, CP-1A company profile). The terms of that affiliate receivable and the guarantor perimeter by instrument are not supplied, which limits any view of how value flows between American and its parent.

cells.text: Major network air carrier providing scheduled passenger and cargo air transportation through hubs in Charlotte, Chicago, Dallas/Fort Worth, Los Angeles, Miami, New York, Philadelphia, Phoenix and Washington, D.C., to over 350 destinations; about 224 million passengers boarded in 2025
Hub scale supports connecting-traffic revenue but ties results to airport, weather and air-traffic disruption at a few nodes

American is the mainline operating subsidiary and issuer; AAG is the holding company that also owns the wholly-owned regional carriers Envoy, PSA and Piedmont, so regional operations sit under AAG and are paid for by American through capacity purchase style arrangements
Issuer cash flows depend on affiliate arrangements and intercompany balances (see CP-1 row for related-party receivables of American)
Passenger, cargo and other revenue, where other revenue is driven largely by the loyalty program; passenger revenue is the dominant stream (CP-1 rows for total operating revenues FY2025 and Q3 2026)
Revenue is cyclical and discretionary on the passenger side; loyalty and cargo add a less volatile layer
Q3 2026 passenger revenue growth was driven by yield (up 18.3%) with load factor down 2.6 points and capacity up 4.2%
Revenue growth in the latest quarter came from price, not volume; price strength can reverse if demand softens while fuel stays high
Management says premium products generate roughly half of ticket revenue on approximately 30% of seats and managed corporate revenue grew 27.6%
Premium and corporate revenue is typically more margin-resilient, but this is a management characterisation and is not verified in the filings

AAdvantage and co-branded credit cards are described as material assets; cash payments from co-branded credit card and other partners were 6.2 billion in 2025; Citi became exclusive U.S. issuer of the co-branded portfolio in 2026; Mastercard extended as exclusive payment network under a 10-year contract from July 2025
Partner cash is a large, recurring inflow that supports liquidity and secures the AAdvantage Financing; a partner change is a counterparty concentration point
Loyalty program liability and air traffic liability together were 20,928 at September 30, 2026 against 17,722 at December 31, 2025
Customer-funded float lifts reported liquidity but reverses if bookings or mileage sales fall, and loyalty liability is a non-debt claim on future revenue
Fuel is among the largest single costs; no fuel hedges were outstanding at September 30, 2026 and the company policy is not to hedge; Q3 2026 average fuel price per gallon rose 62.7% year on year
Unhedged fuel passes price swings straight to operating income and cash flow; revenue recapture is partial and lagged

Salaries, wages and benefits were 38% of 2025 operating expenses; about 139,100 FTE at year end 2025, about 86% unionized; mainline pilot, mechanic and fleet service contracts become amendable in 2027
Labor is the largest cost and largely fixed in the short run; 2027 amendable dates are a cost-reset and disruption risk inside the debt maturity window

Regional flying is under capacity purchase agreements in which American receives all revenue and pays predetermined fees plus 100% of certain variable costs such as landing fees, fuel and insurance; 42% of regional passengers connected to or from mainline
Regional capacity is a fixed commitment that does not flex with passenger volume, and fuel is borne by American
American holds a 20.8% equity interest in Republic Holdings, parent of a capacity purchase partner; a 78 impairment was recorded in Q3 2026 and carrying value fell to 187
Equity exposure to a supplier adds a small capital loss risk and ties to the same counterparty that is paid under the capacity agreement

Definitive purchase agreements for 365 new aircraft at September 30, 2026; management guided to 49 deliveries in 2026 and total capex of about 4 billion in the April deck; aircraft and engine purchase commitments of American total 24,056 (CP-1 row)
Fleet commitments are fixed, front-loaded financing needs; the company says it intends to finance deliveries with cash and long-term financing, so aircraft-backed debt keeps being added
Mainline fleet of 1,013 aircraft at December 31, 2025, of which 547 owned and 466 leased; 567 regional aircraft operated
Owned aircraft are the collateral base for EETC and equipment financing; leased aircraft add operating lease claims
Negative working capital structure: current liabilities exceeded current assets, driven by air traffic liability and loyalty liability
Operating cash flow in the period was helped by float build, which is seasonal; discrete Q3 operating cash flow was negative (CP-1 calculation C7)

Non-fuel cost growth came from wages (5.7%), selling expenses (14.7%), other rent and landing fees (9.9%) and other operating expenses (13.7%); management CASM excluding special items, fuel and profit sharing rose 3.0%
Cost pressure beyond fuel limits operating leverage on revenue gains

Management expects fourth quarter 2026 revenue growth of 19.5% to 22.5%, an adjusted loss per share for the year, and a fuel price assumption of about 4.70 per gallon; it states fuel is a headwind of about 7 billion year over year
Guidance is a forecast and not a result; it shows management itself does not expect a full year adjusted profit

runs.text: Strengths. Liquidity: USD 11,763 million at American and USD 11,797 million at AAG, up from USD 9,233 million at December 31, 2025 at AAG, with no revolver draw, gives the issuer time to absorb a fuel shock (Documentary Fact). Financing access: the issuer raised about USD 4,100 million of aircraft-backed debt in the first nine months of 2026, repaid USD 1,000 million of 8.50% secured notes and a USD 629 million term loan, and extended its largest bank maturities, which shows market access and lowers near-term refinancing risk (Documentary Fact). Franchise and cash generation from loyalty partners, with USD 6,200 million of partner cash in 2025, supports revenue visibility and collateral value (Documentary Fact; Management Language for the premium and corporate growth claims). Capital allocation: no dividends or share repurchases in 2025 or 2024, and prepayments of expensive secured debt in 2026, are creditor-supportive actions (Documentary Fact). Scale and network: nine hubs, over 350 destinations and a mainline fleet in which 547 of 1,013 aircraft are owned give a large collateral base for asset-backed financing (Documentary Fact).

Weaknesses. Earnings and coverage: operating income is near break-even in the latest quarter and below net interest on a last-twelve-month basis (Documentary Fact; Analyst Interpretation for the coverage ratios). Unhedged fuel exposure: the company states it does not hedge and fuel price per gallon rose 62.7% in the third quarter, with management guiding to a full-year adjusted loss per share (Documentary Fact; Management Language for the guidance). Leverage: management net debt of USD 28,079 million against a stated 3.0x target is a long way from target, and the company is still adding secured aircraft debt to fund USD 24,056 million of aircraft and engine purchase commitments (Documentary Fact). Cost inflation outside fuel: management's CASM excluding special items, fuel and profit sharing rose 3.0% while load factor fell 2.6 points, and mainline pilot, mechanic and fleet service contracts become amendable in 2027, inside the debt maturity window (Documentary Fact; Management Language for the CASM measure). Structural subordination: the unsecured PSP notes sit at the parent and American's own creditors rank against encumbered assets whose value is not disclosed (Analyst Interpretation). Transparency: covenant thresholds, executed documents and affiliate balance terms are not in the supplied sources, so covenant headroom cannot be tested (Insufficient Information).

blocks.title: Transaction summary and new debt issues

runs.text: There is no single acquisition, buyout or recapitalisation transaction in the supplied sources; the transaction record is a sequence of refinancings and aircraft financings. No sponsor, use of proceeds beyond general fleet financing, or dividend recapitalisation is documented. Status of every item below is completed as of September 30, 2026 unless stated.

New debt issued or amended in 2026, taken from the third quarter 10-Q note on debt (Q3 page:16 to page:20): in February 2026 the 2025 AAdvantage Term Loan Facility was replaced in the same principal amount with a lower margin by the AAdvantage Issuers (American and AAdvantage Loyalty IP Ltd.); in March 2026 the 2013, 2014 and 2023 revolving facilities were reset with maturities in March 2031 and an aggregate size that management says rose from 3.0 billion to 3.1 billion, and a separate 350 revolver was extended to March 2028; in March 2026 American borrowed 870 under junior Class (B)R aircraft EETC financing at a fixed 5.61%, maturing 2028 to 2029; in May 2026 the 2014 term loans due January 2027 were refinanced to May 2033 with 703 of incremental term loans at a margin of 3.00% over SOFR; in May 2026 the 2026-1 aircraft EETCs of about 1.1 billion were issued; in June 2026 the 2026 Engine EETCs of 567 were issued, refinancing 228 of 2019-1 Engine EETCs and adding 339 of new borrowing; in August 2026 the 2026-2 aircraft EETCs of about 1.3 billion were issued, of which about 633 remained in escrow at quarter end and are not reported as American debt; and 705 of variable rate equipment loans were borrowed in the first nine months. Repayments in 2026 include the 629 senior short-term term loan and the 8.50% senior secured notes of 1.0 billion, plus 310 of EETC equipment notes prepaid.

Mechanics for a creditor: the 2026 activity extended the largest bank maturities (2014 term loans to 2033, revolvers to 2031) and replaced a 1.0 billion high-coupon secured note with lower-rate secured debt, which reduces near-term maturity pressure; at the same time it added secured aircraft debt, so more of the fleet is encumbered and unsecured creditors, the AAG-level PSP noteholders, rank behind a larger secured pool. Because nearly all debt is secured by identified collateral, loss given default for any single instrument depends on the collateral package and appraisal, which the sources do not provide; no recovery conclusion is drawn. The October 2026 option exercise for five Airbus A320 Family aircraft and the commitment to buy two Boeing 777-200ER aircraft off-lease in the fourth quarter of 2026 (Q3 page:65) are subsequent events to the September 30 balance sheet and are not included in the period facts above.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: American Airlines, Inc. is a large, liquid but heavily indebted network carrier whose current earnings are too thin to service its debt without continued access to secured financing. The strongest support is USD 11,763 million of available liquidity at September 30, 2026, with nothing drawn on revolving facilities and almost all debt backed by identified collateral. The weakest point is unhedged fuel: a 62.7% higher fuel price per gallon cut third-quarter operating income to USD 115 million on USD 16,335 million of revenue, and last-twelve-month EBITDA covered net interest only 1.74x. The outcome turns on fuel prices, whether yield-led revenue holds, and the USD 7,861 million of principal due in 2028. Confidence is Medium (Analyst Interpretation). [CP-1 table; CP-1A operating model]

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: First, earnings are the pressure point, not liquidity. Revenue grew 19.3% in the third quarter of 2026 to USD 16,335 million, but fuel expense rose USD 1,868 million to USD 4,635 million and operating income fell to USD 115 million from USD 151 million; the pre-tax loss widened to USD 334 million from USD 142 million (Documentary Fact; CP-1 table). Nine-month operating income was USD 521 million against USD 1,015 million a year earlier. The mechanism is that the company carries no fuel hedges and recaptures higher fuel only through fares, so a fuel move reaches operating income and cash flow within the same quarter (Documentary Fact; CP-1A operating model).

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Second, leverage is high on every measure the sources allow. Management's own net debt was USD 28,079 million at September 30, 2026, up from USD 27,438 million at March 31, 2026; against last-twelve-month EBITDAR built from income statement lines of USD 4,127 million that is 6.80x, versus management's stated target of 3.0x (Documentary Fact for the debt figures, Analyst Interpretation for the ratio; CP-1 calculation C13). The ratio omits regional depreciation and rent, so management's own adjusted measure would differ, but the gap to the target is large on any definition the sources support. This also corrects a garbled bullet in the CP-1 handoff, which should have said that net debt rose between those dates.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Third, debt service rests on liquidity and refinancing access more than on earnings. Last-twelve-month operating income of USD 973 million was below net interest expense of USD 1,664 million, and last-twelve-month free cash flow on a simple definition was negative USD 91 million (Documentary Fact; CP-1 calculations C6 and C8). Nine-month operating cash flow of USD 4,541 million was helped by a rise in air traffic and loyalty liabilities, and the derived third-quarter operating cash flow was negative USD 153 million with third-quarter capex of USD 1,095 million (Analyst Interpretation; CP-1 calculation C7). Customer-funded float lifts liquidity in good quarters and unwinds when bookings or mileage sales slow.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Fourth, the maturity profile is manageable near term and concentrated in 2028. American's principal due is USD 631 million for the remainder of 2026, USD 3,550 million in 2027 and USD 7,861 million in 2028, the peak year, against USD 11,797 million of AAG liquidity (Documentary Fact; CP-1 table). Nearly 87% of Note 5 debt is secured (CP-1 calculation C11), and 2026 refinancings pushed the 2014 term loans to May 2033 and revolvers to March 2031, so refinancing depends mainly on asset-backed markets for aircraft and loyalty collateral (Documentary Fact; CP-1A transaction summary). Nothing in the supplied sources shows how much headroom those collateral pools have.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Fifth, the business has real franchise support. Cash from co-branded credit card and other partners was USD 6,200 million in 2025, Citi became exclusive issuer of the co-branded portfolio in 2026, and premium and corporate revenue are growing per management (Documentary Fact for the partner cash, Management Language for the premium claims; CP-1A operating model). That cash is also the collateral base of the AAdvantage Financing, so it supports both revenue durability and secured borrowing capacity.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Sixth, structure matters for this issuer. The three PSP promissory notes of USD 3,746 million are the only unsecured debt and sit at the AAG parent, while American itself carries USD 25,876 million of debt and finance leases and a USD 10,430 million receivable from related parties (Documentary Fact; CP-1 table, CP-1A company profile). The terms of that affiliate receivable and the guarantor perimeter by instrument are not supplied, which limits any view of how value flows between American and its parent.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Strengths. Liquidity: USD 11,763 million at American and USD 11,797 million at AAG, up from USD 9,233 million at December 31, 2025 at AAG, with no revolver draw, gives the issuer time to absorb a fuel shock (Documentary Fact). Financing access: the issuer raised about USD 4,100 million of aircraft-backed debt in the first nine months of 2026, repaid USD 1,000 million of 8.50% secured notes and a USD 629 million term loan, and extended its largest bank maturities, which shows market access and lowers near-term refinancing risk (Documentary Fact). Franchise and cash generation from loyalty partners, with USD 6,200 million of partner cash in 2025, supports revenue visibility and collateral value (Documentary Fact; Management Language for the premium and corporate growth claims). Capital allocation: no dividends or share repurchases in 2025 or 2024, and prepayments of expensive secured debt in 2026, are creditor-supportive actions (Documentary Fact). Scale and network: nine hubs, over 350 destinations and a mainline fleet in which 547 of 1,013 aircraft are owned give a large collateral base for asset-backed financing (Documentary Fact).

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Weaknesses. Earnings and coverage: operating income is near break-even in the latest quarter and below net interest on a last-twelve-month basis (Documentary Fact; Analyst Interpretation for the coverage ratios). Unhedged fuel exposure: the company states it does not hedge and fuel price per gallon rose 62.7% in the third quarter, with management guiding to a full-year adjusted loss per share (Documentary Fact; Management Language for the guidance). Leverage: management net debt of USD 28,079 million against a stated 3.0x target is a long way from target, and the company is still adding secured aircraft debt to fund USD 24,056 million of aircraft and engine purchase commitments (Documentary Fact). Cost inflation outside fuel: management's CASM excluding special items, fuel and profit sharing rose 3.0% while load factor fell 2.6 points, and mainline pilot, mechanic and fleet service contracts become amendable in 2027, inside the debt maturity window (Documentary Fact; Management Language for the CASM measure). Structural subordination: the unsecured PSP notes sit at the parent and American's own creditors rank against encumbered assets whose value is not disclosed (Analyst Interpretation). Transparency: covenant thresholds, executed documents and affiliate balance terms are not in the supplied sources, so covenant headroom cannot be tested (Insufficient Information).
